  • a solid. A primary electron loses energy by exciting a phonon and

  • solid and gradually excite the phonons and hence heat the solid.

  • electrons and hence can be used to study the material properties.

questions.solution_html:
• Give a short note on principle of Differential Thermal Analysis. [U] / [CO4]
  • Ans.
  • DTA measures the temperature difference (ΔT) between a sample and an
  • inert reference material as both are subjected to the same controlled
  • heating or cooling program. The reference undergoes no thermal events,
  • so any deviation in ΔT indicates a thermal event in the sample. The DTA
  • curve is a plot of ΔT versus reference temperature or time. Endothermic
  • events (e.g., melting) appear as downward peaks and exothermic events
  • (e.g., crystallization) as upward peaks in a DTA curve.

questions.question: Distinguish between conventional Differential Scanning Calorimetry and temperature-modulated Differential Scanning Calorimetry. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the solid phase transformation and thermal
  • decomposition.Give example.
  • [A] /
  • [CO4]
  • Ans. • Solid phase transformation refers to a first-order transition in
  • which a material changes its crystal structure without melting.
  • Such transitions involve an enthalpy change and are therefore
  • detectable by DTA and DSC as peaks in the thermal curve. The
  • curve peaks of DTA and DSC readily reveal solid-state phase
  • transformations over a temperature range.
  • • For example pure iron changes its crystal structure from body-centered cubic
  • (BCC) to face-centered cubic (FCC) when the temperature increases to 912 ◦C..
  • • Thermal decomposition is the chemical breakdown of a material
  • upon heating, resulting in a mass change (usually mass loss due to
  • release of volatile products). It is primarily studied using
  • thermogravimetry (TG), where the sample mass is continuously
  • monitored as a function of temperature. Decomposition is
  • characterized by two temperatures: Tᵢ (onset of mass change) and
  • Tf (completion of mass change).
  • • For example, solid CaCO3 will decompose to form solid
  • CaO and gaseous CO2 over a certain temperature range.
  • • Both phenomena can be studied simultaneously using combined
  • TG-DSC/DTA techniques. While TG monitors mass change
  • (decomposition), DSC/DTA monitors heat flow (both phase
  • transformation and decomposition). For example, in polymer
  • composite analysis, TG reveals decomposition temperatures and
  • ceramic content (as in HA/UHMWPE composites, Figure 10.32),
  • while DSC can reveal any solid-state phase transitions occurring
  • within the same temperature range. Together, they provide a
  • comprehensive thermal characterization of a material.
